record.answer:
A Roth IRA and a 401(k) differ in several ways:

- **Contributions**: Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax dollars, while traditional 401(k) contributions are made with pre-tax dollars.
- **Income Limits**: There are income limits for contributing to a Roth IRA, but no income limits for contributing to a 401(k).
- **Contribution Limits**: The annual contribution limit for a Roth IRA is $7,000 ($6,500 for those under 50), while for a 401(k) it is $23,000 ($30,500 for those over 50).
- **Taxation of Withdrawals**: Roth IRA withdrawals are tax-free if they are qualified, while 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as income.
- **Required Distributions**: Roth IRAs do not require minimum distributions during the owner's lifetime, whereas 401(k)s do.

This is general information, not financial advice.

sources.section: Roth 401(k), Roth IRA, and pre-tax 401(k) retirement accounts
sources.text:
Contributions — Designated Roth 401(k): Designated Roth employee elective contributions are made with after-tax dollars.; Roth IRA: Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax dollars.; Pre-tax 401(k): Traditional, pre-tax employee elective contributions are made with before-tax dollars.

Income limits — Designated Roth 401(k): No income limitation to participate.; Roth IRA: Income limits: 2024 – modified AGI married $240,000/single $161,000, 2023 – modified AGI married $228,000/single $153,000, 2022 – modified AGI married $214,000/single $144,000, 2021 - modified AGI married $208,000/single $140,000; Pre-tax 401(k): No income limitation to participate.

Maximum elective contribution — Designated Roth 401(k): Aggregate* employee elective contributions limited to $23,000 in 2024; $22,500 in 2023; $20,500 in 2022; $19,500 in 2021 (plus an additional $6,500 in 2022 and 2021 for employees age 50 or over; additional $7,500 in 2023 and 2024 for employees age 50 or over).; Roth IRA: Contribution limited to $7,000 plus an additional $1,000 for employees age 50 or older in 2024; $6,500 plus an additional $1,000 for employees age 50 or older in 2023; $6,000 plus an additional $1,000 for employees age 50 or over in 2021 and 2022.; Pre-tax 401(k): Same aggregate* limit as designated Roth 401(k) account

Taxation of withdrawals — Designated Roth 401(k): Withdrawals of contributions and earnings are not taxed provided it’s a qualified distribution – the account is held for at least 5 years and made: On account of disability,, On or after death, or, On or after attainment of age 59½.; Roth IRA: Same as designated Roth 401(k) account and can have a qualified distribution for a first-time home purchase.; Pre-tax 401(k): Withdrawals of contributions and earnings are subject to federal and most state income taxes.

Required distributions — Designated Roth 401(k): Distributions must begin no later than age 72 (age 70 ½ if reached age 70 ½ before January 1, 2020), unless still working and not a 5% owner.; Roth IRA: No requirement to start taking distributions while owner is alive.; Pre-tax 401(k): Same as designated Roth 401(k) account.

sources.title: Roth IRAs | Internal Revenue Service
sources.text:
A Roth IRA is an IRA that, except as explained below, is subject to the rules that apply to a traditional IRA.

-
You cannot deduct contributions to a Roth IRA.
-
If you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions are tax-free.
-
You can make contributions to your Roth IRA after you reach age 70 ½.
-
You can leave amounts in your Roth IRA as long as you live.
-
The account or annuity must be designated as a Roth IRA when it is set up.

The same combined contribution limit applies to all of your Roth and traditional IRAs.
